title: Giving instructions
practiceFocus: Give five instructions, mixing tú and usted

points.title: Informal borrows a form you know
points.rule: For an informal tú affirmative command, use the él/ella present form: habla, come, escribe. A handful are irregular: di, ve, ten, pon, sal, sé, ven. A negative tú command, and any usted command, uses a different set of endings. Learn the common ones here as fixed phrases, the same way es and está stayed chunks before their charts.
points.pattern: tú: él/ella form (corta) · no + switched vowel (no cortes) · usted: switched vowel (hable)

examples.english: Usted, affirmative. Speak more slowly, please.

tips: Pronouns attach to the end of a positive command and go before a negative one: pruébalo, no lo cocines.
Use tú in a recipe or with a friend. Use usted with a stranger or a doctor.

mistakes.why: A negative tú command switches the vowel: -ar verbs take -es.
In a negative command the pronoun goes before the verb.

grammar.notYet: The full command chart for every verb type. Learn these shapes next to the phrases, and build the pattern later.

phrases.spanish: Corta las verduras en trozos pequeños.
phrases.english: Cut the vegetables into small pieces.

phrases.spanish: Siga todo recto y gire a la izquierda.

phrases.note: Usted, a recipe or an offer.

lines.speaker: Abuela
lines.spanish: Añade aceite y espera cinco minutos. No lo cocines a fuego muy alto.
lines.english: Add oil and wait five minutes. Don’t cook it on too high a heat.

lines.speaker: Abuela
lines.spanish: Sí. Ten cuidado, está caliente. Añade sal al final.
lines.english: Yes. Be careful, it is hot. Add salt at the end.

lines.speaker: Alex
lines.english: Thanks, grandma. I am going to try it.

practice.title: Five instructions
practice.instruction: Give five instructions: three informal tú commands, such as steps in a simple recipe or advice to a friend, and two formal usted commands, such as directions or an offer to a stranger.
tips: Say who you are speaking to before you choose the form.
A friend gets tú. A stranger, or someone you address formally, gets usted.
